passage: Wanjiru held her phone up in the school yard in Nairobi. "Everyone in Form Two is trying this, Vera. The creator says a bottle of this energy powder makes you unstoppable." She lowered her voice. "But don't tell your mum, or the teachers. That's the rule of the group." Vera liked the idea of belonging, and she liked Wanjiru. Still, something in her stomach twisted at the word 'secret'. She glanced at the video again; nobody said what was in it. "Let me think," she said, smiling so Wanjiru wouldn't feel rejected. That evening she told her mother about the powder and the secret rule. Her mother did not laugh. "Thank you for telling me. Let's read what it says together tomorrow."

qa.q: Where did Wanjiru show Vera the video?
qa.a: She showed it in the school yard in Nairobi.

qa.q: Why did Vera feel uneasy even though she wanted to belong?
qa.a: The word 'secret' made her uncomfortable, and nobody in the video said what was in the powder. She also wanted to keep Wanjiru's friendship, so her feelings were mixed.

qa.q: What step would help Vera most from here?
qa.a: Telling a trusted adult, as she did, and checking the facts about the powder together before deciding anything.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru see Vera's answer of 'let me think'?
qa.a: She may feel a bit hurt or worried about being left out, or she may just accept it as a normal pause.

grounding: A teen weighs a peer and influencer recommendation that carries secrecy, and consults a trusted adult.

passage: The hostel common room smelled of instant noodles. Hansa sat on the arm of the sofa scrolling. "Santosh, you have to see this. A famous streamer says you should share your live location with everyone in the group and not let the warden know. It's just for fun, everyone does it." Santosh watched the little video. Half of him wanted to be the cool one who joined. The other half kept thinking about strangers in the group. "Who are the people in it?" he asked. Hansa shrugged. "Some are friends of friends." He said nothing for a moment. "I'm going to ask Ms Iyer first." "Don't be boring," Hansa said, but she also didn't stop him. He left, phone in hand.

qa.q: What smell filled the hostel common room?
qa.a: The common room smelled of instant noodles.

qa.q: What might Santosh be worried about when he asks who is in the group?
qa.a: He felt drawn to being the cool one who joined, but he worried about strangers seeing his live location and about the rule to hide it from the warden. His question suggests he wanted facts before deciding.

qa.q: What could Santosh do next?
qa.a: Talk to Ms Iyer or another trusted adult about the request before sharing anything, as he says he will.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel when Santosh says he will ask Ms Iyer?
qa.a: She may feel annoyed at being called out or worried about being teased, but she does not stop him, so she may also be unsure herself. 🤔

grounding: Peer and influencer advice with pressure and secrecy is a reason to consult a trusted adult, shown in a hostel.

passage:
Dear Disha didi,
You said I could write to you about anything, so here goes.
Last week some girls in my building started a trend from a video site: sitting on the edge of the terrace wall for a photo, legs over the side. Sunita said it gets loads of likes and "don't tell anyone, parents freak out." Everyone in our group did it except me. I kept saying maybe tomorrow.
I felt like a coward. But the "don't tell anyone" part kept bothering me.
Yesterday I told Amma. She didn't shout. She went straight to the building secretary that evening, the terrace door was locked by night, and she phoned the other parents too. Sunita is angry with me, but Amma says that anger is safer than a fall.
Was I wrong? Tell me honestly.
Love,
Rukmini

qa.q: What did Sunita say about the terrace photo trend?
qa.a: Sunita said it gets loads of likes and "don't tell anyone, parents freak out."

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling about refusing the trend?
qa.a: Rukmini felt like a coward for not joining, and uneasy about the "don't tell anyone" part. Now Sunita's anger leaves Rukmini torn, still asking if it was wrong.

qa.q: What would you advise Rukmini about her choice?
qa.a: Telling Amma was the right step, because a trend that is dangerous and kept secret is exactly when to go to a trusted adult, even if a friend is upset for a while.

qa.q: How might Sunita see Rukmini's choice right now?
qa.a: Sunita probably feels betrayed and embarrassed, but she may later see that the locked door protected her and the others from a real fall.

grounding: The letter shows a teenager weighing a peer trend that is unsafe and secret, and turning to a trusted adult who acts the same evening.

passage:
Okay, Sangeeta ma'am, since this is the school podcast and you asked about influencers: I'm Ojas, and I follow about fifty people who review games. Most of the time their tips are good. One recommended a headset; my friend Neil bought it; it's great.
But last month a gamer I really liked said, "Get cheap coins on this site, it's legit, just use your parent's card and don't mention it." And my friends were all like, "He's never wrong."
I nearly did it. Honestly. What stopped me was the "don't mention it." Good tips don't need hiding.
So I showed my dad that same night. He checked and said the site looked like a scam that steals card details. He reported it and blocked it on our home internet.
Now I still watch that gamer, but I don't just trust everything he says.

qa.q: Which product did Neil buy on a reviewer's recommendation?
qa.a: Neil bought a headset, and it's great.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when the gamer told viewers not to mention the site?
qa.a: Ojas was tempted, since the gamer was a favourite, but uneasy about the secrecy. That doubt made Ojas careful enough to check with Dad.

qa.q: What small step helped Ojas weigh the recommendation?
qa.a: Noticing that the tip asked for secrecy and showing Dad the same night, so a trusted adult could check the site before any card was used.

qa.q: How might Ojas's friends see the gamer differently from Ojas now?
qa.a: They may still trust him completely, saying "He's never wrong," while Ojas now sees that even a liked influencer can push something unsafe.

grounding: The spoken account shows a teenager weighing recommendations from friends and an influencer, and taking a secret, risky tip to a trusted adult.

passage:
My little brother Ojas plays an online football game most evenings, and I usually hear him shouting at the screen. On Tuesday he was quiet. I noticed because I was on the sofa behind him.
He kept typing in the game chat, deleting, and typing again. Once he looked over his shoulder at me, then turned back fast. I can't know what he was thinking. Maybe he was just losing.
After twenty minutes he came and sat next to me. "Abhinav bhaiya, a guy in my team says he'll give me rare players free if I send him my number. He says his older friends recommend him. But he said don't tell my parents."
I told him he'd done exactly right by telling me. We went to Mummy together straight away. She helped Ojas block and report the account, and we changed his settings so strangers can't message him.
He played again after dinner, shouting as usual.

qa.q: How long did Ojas type and delete before coming to sit with Abhinav?
qa.a: After twenty minutes Ojas came and sat next to Abhinav.

qa.q: What might Ojas's quiet typing and glance over his shoulder suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Ojas felt uneasy and torn between the tempting offer and the request for secrecy. Abhinav admits it could also have been frustration at losing.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do well when Ojas told him?
qa.a: He praised Ojas for speaking up and took him straight to Mummy, so a trusted adult could block and report the contact that same evening.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about Ojas coming forward?
qa.a: She would probably feel relieved and proud that Ojas told his brother instead of keeping the secret the contact asked for.

grounding: The older brother's account shows a teenager weighing a stranger's recommendation that carries secrecy and turning to trusted family.

passage:
Saturday. Trisha sent Sabina three videos: a lip balm that "changed her life", a study playlist, and a creator's "no-sleep streak", where you stay up all night on a group video call and post proof at dawn. "Tried the playlist, it's good," Sabina typed. "The streak looks fun?"
Tuesday. Trisha added Sabina to a group called "24h club". The pinned message said: Don't tell parents, they'll ruin it. Loser if you drop out. Sabina's stomach turned at "don't tell". The playlist had never needed secrecy.
Thursday. After dinner Sabina showed the group to Chachi, who was ironing uniforms. Chachi read it twice, put the iron down and said, "I'm glad you showed me. Let's leave this group together now, and I'll call Trisha's mother tonight so she isn't pushed into it either." Sabina left the group, then messaged Trisha: "Not doing it. Chachi's calling your mum, not to get you in trouble."

qa.q: What did the pinned message in the group say?
qa.a: It said: Don't tell parents, they'll ruin it. Loser if you drop out.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she read 'don't tell'?
qa.a: Sabina felt uneasy and wary, her stomach turning, because the playlist had never needed secrecy. There may also have been some worry about being called a loser for leaving.

qa.q: How did Chachi's response help?
qa.a: Chachi thanked Sabina, left the group with her that same evening and called Trisha's mother that night, so Trisha wasn't pressured either.

qa.q: How might Trisha see the videos differently from Sabina?
qa.a: Trisha seems to see all three as fun recommendations, the streak no different from the playlist, so she may not have noticed the pressure and secrecy in it.

grounding: It shows a teenager weighing recommendations from a peer and a creator, and turning to a trusted adult when one of them comes with secrecy and pressure.
